article_content: The deadly Ebola virus has been contracted within the United States for the first time. A nurse wearing protective gear during extensive contact at a Dallas hospital with Ebola patient Thomas Eric Duncan, who later died, tested positive in a preliminary blood test, officials confirmed Sunday. Despite using a gown, gloves, mask, and face shield during multiple interactions with Duncan, health officials identified a protocol breach. The nurse works at Texas Health Presbyterian Hospital, per a source briefed on the case. The CDC confirmed the diagnosis Sunday, marking the first U.S. transmission and second domestic case. CDC Director Tom Frieden noted the nurse cared for Duncan after his isolation following his second hospital visit—post-Liberian travel. The nurse remains stable, reported Texas Health Resources' Dan Varga. Dallas hazardous materials teams decontaminated public areas near her apartment, with proactive isolation of a close contact. The CDC underscored that community spread can be contained through rigorous contact tracing and immediate isolation of symptomatic individuals. Officials anticipated this possibility, highlighting preparedness efforts. After reporting a low-grade fever Friday, the nurse was isolated. President Obama directed federal agencies to bolster Ebola protocol enforcement. Experts framed the rapid detection as a system success despite Ebola's global toll (over 8,300 cases, 4,000 deaths in West Africa).

article_content: A police officer falsely accused an innocent banker of assault in a retaliatory bid to frame him after the banker allegedly criticized police funding, a court heard. PC Jason Cooke, 42, claimed Anthony Jordine pushed him into a shop window in Brick Lane, east London, breaking it. Prosecutors argued Cooke lunged at Jordine before he was forcibly restrained and kicked. The incident occurred late on February 26, 2022. Jurors were told Jordine made a comment about funding police salaries during a traffic stop, prompting Cooke to fabricate allegations. Despite initial arrests for assault and criminal damage, CCTV evidence led to charges being dropped and a new investigation into Cooke's conduct. Cooke denies perverting justice and described the encounter as a misunderstanding.

article_content: To mark the centenary of Germany's 1914 naval attack on Scarborough, the historic coastal town will hold solemn ceremonies honoring the 18 civilians killed and 200 injured. Events include a dawn service at Scarborough Castle where a traditional maroon signal will precede readings of victims' names. A harbor flotilla and newly unveiled memorial cairn at Manor Road Cemetery will also feature. Historian Michael Knaggs highlights how the government exploited the December 16 attack's emotional impact through recruitment campaigns like 'Remember Scarborough!' The early-morning timing likely prevented greater school-related casualties, though 14-month-old John Shields Ryalls' death prompted Churchill's condemnation of 'baby killers.' Over 200 buildings were damaged when the German fleet fired 776 shells in 29 minutes. While Hartlepool suffered greater losses, Scarborough's prominence as a luxury resort made it ideal for propaganda purposes. The Bennetts, a family of four killed in their Wykeham Street home, became central to recruitment imagery. This attack marked the first significant German strike on British soil, spurring retaliatory calls like 'Avenge Scarborough!'

article_content: Japanese Prime Minister Naoto Kan announced Tuesday he will stop receiving his prime minister's salary of ¥1.6 million monthly until the Fukushima nuclear emergency ends. Alongside this gesture, he committed to revisiting Japan's energy policies to expand renewable energy use. While maintaining his lawmaker's income, Kan emphasized solidarity with citizens enduring the crisis. The move coincided with a brief evacuation zone access period: roughly 100 Kawauchi villagers donned protective suits to revisit homes abandoned since April 22. Allowed only two hours to collect essentials - including vital medications for those with long-term health conditions - residents underwent radiation screening afterward. Authorities mentioned possible future trips to retrieve pets left behind. The March 11 disaster's tsunami crippled Fukushima's cooling systems, causing reactor meltdowns and releasing dangerous radiation. Approximately 78,000 residents remain evacuated from a 20km exclusion zone, while another 60,000 in adjacent areas continue sheltering indoors.
